3.text: these tribes supply assistants for the Chukchee herds. Thus Araˊro has Tungus

4.text: assistants in all four herds belonging to him. This became possible, of course,

5.text: only during the last fifty years, when peace was assured, and the tribes began

6.text: to intermingle, at least on their common frontiers. The admission of Tungus

7.text: assistants is quite natural, as the Chukchee herds of those localities are full

8.text: of Tungus reindeer, which are more valuable, and the care and breaking of

9.text: which are better known to the Tungus. Especially is this the case in the

10.text: summer-time and with riding-reindeer, since the Chukchee have no experience

11.text: in dealing with these. Some young Chukchee breeders take a Tungus assistant,

12.text: purposely for the summer-time, in order to learn from him the ways of riding

13.text: reindeer and of wandering in summer. In many cases, however, Tungus

14.text: assistants do not stay very long in the Chukchee camps, the character of both

15.text: tribes being so different. The Chukchee does not like much wandering, but

16.text: he is ever mindful of the increasc of his animals. This care requires great

17.text: alertness and uninterrupted attention to the herd and pasture. The Tungus

18.text: is indolent, and soon wearies of camp duties. He likes travel and hunting,

19.text: and is altogether of a roaming disposition. So, after a few months, he often

20.text: leaves the Chukchee camp, which is heavy and too stationary for his tastes,

21.text: and wanders far away to hunt wild reindeer or mountain-sheep.

22.text: Paupers. — The Chukchee camp knows hardly any other social position

23.text: than that of the master, his nearest relatives, and his assistants. Later I

24.text: shall speak of the Maritime village, which is founded on another principle,

25.text: that of territorial contiguity, and which is much larger than the camp. I shall

26.text: indicate then the elements of population of different character; for instance,

27.text: very poor families, consisting mostly of widows and orphans, who have no

28.text: near relatives, and who depend for their support wholly on their neighbors.

29.text: The Chukchee camp rarely knows such categories of people. All families of

30.text: the Reindeer Chukchee are connected among themselves by ties of relationship.

31.text: Thus a poor family without relatives is almost impossible. Nearly always

32.text: some relative, however distant, will take them to his camp and give them

33.text: means for subsistence. Even when an assistant living in the camp of another

34.text: man suddenly dies, his family, though not at all related to the master, will

35.text: be kept in the camp and provided for, however sparingly. On the other

36.text: hand, a family utterly friendless, and strangers to every one, are placed in a

37.text: very difficult position, since they have no place in which to live. Of course,

38.text: when a stranger family happens to come to a Chukchee camp, — for instance,

39.text: during the trade-gatherings, — if they are poor and have no reindeer of their

40.text: own to slaughter, the master of the camp, when he slaughters for his people,

41.text: may also slaughter an animal for the poor visitors. In times of ceremonial

42.text: slaughtering, even Russian and Tungus guests receive slaughtered fawns as a

43.text: present from the master of the camp.
